newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian stocks fly sky high, no end in sight.
newsitem.headline: Croatian stocks fly sky high, no end in sight.

text.p: Just two years after it was founded, Croatia's stock market has turned into the darling of the region's fledgling bourses, and analysts said on Friday an end to the recent buying frenzy was not in sight.

In a mere 40 days since August, shares of five firms surged ahead 100 percent and more, including a record gain of well over 200 percent by hotel operator Riviera. Turnover last month was up 56 percent from August, while volume jumped 65 percent.
"The market is likely to keep rising for a while," said James Oates, director of central and eastern Europe at UBS in London, adding a correction was not expected before sometime next year.
"After a period of such sharp growth, the market will take a breather sometime next year. There will be some volatility but I don't think it's immediate," he added.

Hotels, particularly those on Istrian peninsula, have led the advance as investor confidence grows that tourists will return to the country's picturesque coast after a four-year lull when war in neighbouring Bosnia made Croatia an unattractive destination to all but the most daring travellers.
Arenaturist tripled in value since August to 290 kuna, Jadranturist added 150 percent, Istraturist rose to 300 from 140 kuna, and Laguna almost doubled its value to close at 1,550 kuna on Thursday.
Reflecting the success of Istrian companies, hotelier Suncani Hvar on the Dalmatian coast jumped from 45 to 115 kuna in just one week.

Speculation by domestic investors that some of the top gainers will follow the lead of drug maker Pliva and Zagrebacka Banka, the country's top bank, and list their stocks on the London Stock Exchange have added fuel to the recent bull run.
Pliva, the first eastern European company to list its shares internationally, and Zagrebacka Banka have risen six to seven times in value since blazing the way earlier this year.
Such gains have convinced small domestic investors, unfamiliar with the idea of putting their meagre savings into the stock market, that the Zagreb bourse may indeed be a bet about to pay off.

"The current trend is based on speculation," said Wolfgang Rigler, Croatia analyst at Raiffeisen Investmentbank in Vienna. "A 50-percent increase in some shares is not based on economic fundamentals."

The most likely candidates for an international listing are thought to be chocolate maker Kras and food processor Podravka, both in talks with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development over new capital injections.

Kras has risen 165 percent since August, closing at 720 kuna on Thursday. Podravka, in the midst of restructuring and still reeling from a stinging loss last year, rose a more modest 53 kuna over the past six weeks to close at 272.90.
Despite such spectacular speculative gains, domestic and foreign analysts agree there is no reason to fear the Zagreb bourse's advance may be a bubble waiting to burst.
"Spectacular gains over the past few months and the media attention that has followed will keep the interest strong," said Velimir Zelimorski of brokerage Fima.
Raiffeisen's Rigler also said he expected the market to continue racing ahead, adding there was "space for some correction during the winter or towards the end of the year".
